title: Stonehenge Altar Stone: Origin Still a Mystery
paragraphs: Among the megaliths of Stonehenge, the Altar Stone, a six-ton slab of sandstone some 4.9 metres long, has proved the most stubbornly evasive about its own beginnings. For the better part of a century orthodoxy placed its source in west Wales, alongside the smaller bluestones that made a journey of about 225 kilometres; later research redirected the inquiry towards north-east Scotland, implying a Neolithic haul of altogether greater ambition.

A fresh analysis, led by Professor Duncan Pirrie of the University of South Wales and published in the Journal of the Geological Society, subjects that revision to scrutiny. Drawing on new observations of the monument and on fragments curated in museum collections, the team reconstructed the stone's geological fingerprint, from its fabric and mineralogy to its geochemistry and isotopic character, and held it against rock formations across Britain, including the Orcadian Basin singled out by earlier work.

The verdict is a qualified one. "So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone," Pirrie said, which narrows the field without closing it: a Scottish origin has been neither confirmed nor excluded, and the true quarry remains unidentified. It is a salutary reminder that in provenance studies the elimination of suspects can be as instructive as the identification of a culprit, though it makes for a less satisfying headline.

questions.q: What does 'evasive' suggest about the stone?
questions.a: It has resisted attempts to identify its origin.

questions.q: What does the study achieve without closing the question?
questions.a: It narrows the field of possible sources.

questions.q: What point does the final sentence make?
questions.a: Eliminating possible sources can be informative even without a definite answer.
